title: Case Study 11: Criminal Safeguards, Arrest & Custodial Rights (Articles 20 & 22) (Article 20(1) — Writ Petition (Civil/Criminal))
legalTheme: Criminal Safeguards, Arrest & Custodial Rights (Articles 20 & 22) • Article 20(1) & Ex Post Facto
factualMatrix: In a matter instituted before the Supreme Court of India (Article 32 Writ Jurisdiction), the Petitioner—an aggrieved citizen/association affected by a recent Legislative Secretariat / Returning Officer action—challenged the constitutionality and procedural validity of an impugned disciplinary dismissal / disqualification order touching upon Article 20(1) (Criminal Safeguards, Arrest & Custodial Rights (Articles 20 & 22)). The Petitioner contended that Core constitutional framework under Criminal Safeguards, Arrest & Custodial Rights (Articles 20 & 22). Further, relying on the evolution of doctrine through Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala (1973), the Petitioner argued that the State failed to satisfy the strict constitutional threshold and acted with manifest arbitrariness.
framingQuestions: 1. Whether the Writ Petition (Civil/Criminal) before the Supreme Court of India (Article 32 Writ Jurisdiction) is maintainable in light of Article 20(1) and constitutional remedies?

2. How does the principle of Criminal Safeguards, Arrest & Custodial Rights (Articles 20 & 22) (Ex Post Facto) apply to the impugned disciplinary dismissal / disqualification order issued by the Legislative Secretariat / Returning Officer?
3. What is the controlling effect of Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala (1973) on the validity of the State/Respondent's action and what relief follows?
statutoryApplicability: Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala (1973)
modelAnswer:
1. MAINTAINABILITY & THRESHOLD (Article 20(1)): Under the constitutional scheme governing Criminal Safeguards, Arrest & Custodial Rights (Articles 20 & 22), a Writ Petition (Civil/Criminal) before the Supreme Court of India (Article 32 Writ Jurisdiction) is maintainable where a prima facie breach of Article 20(1) or statutory/constitutional limits is demonstrated. The Court evaluates threshold jurisdiction without permitting procedural technicalities to defeat substantive constitutional justice.

2. DOCTRINAL & STATUTORY ANALYSIS (Criminal Safeguards, Arrest & Custodial Rights (Articles 20 & 22)): Core constitutional framework under Criminal Safeguards, Arrest & Custodial Rights (Articles 20 & 22). Applying the core concept of 'Ex Post Facto', the impugned disciplinary dismissal / disqualification order by the Legislative Secretariat / Returning Officer must satisfy legality, rational nexus, and proportionality. As reinforced by Article 20(1) has two limbs: (1) no person shall be convicted of any offence except for violation of a law in force at the time of the commission of the act; and (2) no person shall be subjected to a penalty greater than that which might have been inflicted under the law in force at the time.

3. PRECEDENT APPLICATION (Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala (1973)) & RELIEF: Guided by Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala (1973), any executive or legislative overreach inconsistent with Article 20(1) is liable to be struck down or suitably moulded by appropriate directions. Further, In Hathising Mfg. Co. v. UOI (1960), the Supreme Court affirmed that Article 20(1) operates exclusively in the sphere of criminal law; civil obligations, contractual liabilities, and retrospective tax laws do not violate Article 20(1).

MAINTAINABILITY & THRESHOLD (Article 20(2)): Under the constitutional scheme governing Criminal Safeguards, Arrest & Custodial Rights (Articles 20 & 22), a Writ Petition (Art. 226) before the High Court Division Bench (Article 226 Jurisdiction) is maintainable where a prima facie breach of Article 20(2) or statutory/constitutional limits is demonstrated. 2. DOCTRINAL & STATUTORY ANALYSIS (Ex-Post Facto, Double Jeopardy, Self-Incrimination, Written Grounds of Arrest & 2024 Bail Protections): Core constitutional framework under Criminal Safeguards, Arrest & Custodial Rights (Articles 20 & 22). Applying the core concept of 'Double Jeopardy', the impugned impugned legislative bill / ordinance provision by the Disciplinary & Vigilance Authority must satisfy legality, rational nexus, and proportionality. legalTheme: Criminal Safeguards, Arrest & Custodial Rights (Articles 20 & 22) • Article 22(2) & Custodial Remand
factualMatrix: In a matter instituted before the Special Bench / Judicial Magistrate First Class, the Petitioner—an aggrieved citizen/association affected by a recent State Government Department action—challenged the constitutionality and procedural validity of an impugned executive notification and show-cause order touching upon Article 22(2) (Ex-Post Facto, Double Jeopardy, Self-Incrimination, Written Grounds of Arrest & 2024 Bail Protections). The Petitioner contended that Core constitutional framework under Criminal Safeguards, Arrest & Custodial Rights (Articles 20 & 22). Further, relying on the evolution of doctrine through Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala (1973), the Petitioner argued that the State failed to satisfy the strict constitutional threshold and acted with manifest arbitrariness.
framingQuestions: 1. Whether the Criminal Misc. / Remand Application before the Special Bench / Judicial Magistrate First Class is maintainable in light of Article 22(2) and constitutional remedies?

2. How does the principle of Ex-Post Facto, Double Jeopardy, Self-Incrimination, Written Grounds of Arrest & 2024 Bail Protections (Custodial Remand) apply to the impugned executive notification and show-cause order issued by the State Government Department?
3. What is the controlling effect of Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala (1973) on the validity of the State/Respondent's action and what relief follows?
statutoryApplicability: Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala (1973)
modelAnswer:
1. MAINTAINABILITY & THRESHOLD (Article 22(2)): Under the constitutional scheme governing Criminal Safeguards, Arrest & Custodial Rights (Articles 20 & 22), a Criminal Misc. / Remand Application before the Special Bench / Judicial Magistrate First Class is maintainable where a prima facie breach of Article 22(2) or statutory/constitutional limits is demonstrated. The Court evaluates threshold jurisdiction without permitting procedural technicalities to defeat substantive constitutional justice.

2. DOCTRINAL & STATUTORY ANALYSIS (Ex-Post Facto, Double Jeopardy, Self-Incrimination, Written Grounds of Arrest & 2024 Bail Protections): Core constitutional framework under Criminal Safeguards, Arrest & Custodial Rights (Articles 20 & 22). Applying the core concept of 'Custodial Remand', the impugned executive notification and show-cause order by the State Government Department must satisfy legality, rational nexus, and proportionality. As reinforced by Article 22(3) provides that nothing in clauses (1) and (2) shall apply: (a) to any person who for the time being is an enemy alien; or (b) to any person who is arrested or detained under any law providing for preventive detention.

3. PRECEDENT APPLICATION (Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala (1973)) & RELIEF: Guided by Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala (1973), any executive or legislative overreach inconsistent with Article 22(2) is liable to be struck down or suitably moulded by appropriate directions. Further, In the operational bare act text of Article 22(4), no law providing for preventive detention shall authorize detention for a longer period than three months without an Advisory Board opinion. factualMatrix: In a matter instituted before the Special Bench / Judicial Magistrate First Class, the Petitioner—an aggrieved citizen/association affected by a recent State Government Department action—challenged the constitutionality and procedural validity of an impugned executive notification and show-cause order touching upon Article 22(2) (Ex-Post Facto, Double Jeopardy, Self-Incrimination, Written Grounds of Arrest & 2024 Bail Protections). Further, relying on the evolution of doctrine through Kesavananda Bharati v. 2. How does the principle of Ex-Post Facto, Double Jeopardy, Self-Incrimination, Written Grounds of Arrest & 2024 Bail Protections (Default Bail) apply to the impugned executive notification and show-cause order issued by the State Government Department?
3. What is the controlling effect of Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala (1973) on the validity of the State/Respondent's action and what relief follows?

modelAnswer:
1. MAINTAINABILITY & THRESHOLD (Article 22(2)): Under the constitutional scheme governing Criminal Safeguards, Arrest & Custodial Rights (Articles 20 & 22), a Criminal Misc. / Remand Application before the Special Bench / Judicial Magistrate First Class is maintainable where a prima facie breach of Article 22(2) or statutory/constitutional limits is demonstrated. The Court evaluates threshold jurisdiction without permitting procedural technicalities to defeat substantive constitutional justice.

2. DOCTRINAL & STATUTORY ANALYSIS (Ex-Post Facto, Double Jeopardy, Self-Incrimination, Written Grounds of Arrest & 2024 Bail Protections): Core constitutional framework under Criminal Safeguards, Arrest & Custodial Rights (Articles 20 & 22). Applying the core concept of 'Default Bail', the impugned executive notification and show-cause order by the State Government Department must satisfy legality, rational nexus, and proportionality. As reinforced by In Khatri (II) (1981) and Suk Das (1986), the Supreme Court ruled that right to free legal aid is an essential ingredient of reasonable procedure under Article 21, and magistrates have a duty to inform indigent accused. Thus (R) explains (A).

State of Kerala (1973), any executive or legislative overreach inconsistent with Article 22(2) is liable to be struck down or suitably moulded by appropriate directions. Further, All three statements are correct under Ramesh Chandra Mehta (1970 5-Judge Bench). Section 108 Customs Act summons is an inquiry, not an accusation; statements recorded are admissible and not hit by 20(3).

MAINTAINABILITY & THRESHOLD (Article 22(1)): Under the constitutional scheme governing Criminal Safeguards, Arrest & Custodial Rights (Articles 20 & 22), a Constitutional Reference before the Constitution Bench (Article 145(3) Reference) is maintainable where a prima facie breach of Article 22(1) or statutory/constitutional limits is demonstrated. The Court evaluates threshold jurisdiction without permitting procedural technicalities to defeat substantive constitutional justice.

DOCTRINAL & STATUTORY ANALYSIS (Criminal Safeguards, Arrest & Custodial Rights (Articles 20 & 22)): Core constitutional framework under Criminal Safeguards, Arrest & Custodial Rights (Articles 20 & 22). Applying the core concept of 'Arrest Memo', the impugned statutory amendment and implementing rules by the University / Statutory Licensing Board must satisfy legality, rational nexus, and proportionality. As reinforced by Unlike the old Section 167(2) CrPC (under which Anupam Kulkarni held that police custody was permissible only during the first 15 days), Section 187 BNSS explicitly permits police custody to be taken in parts throughout the initial 40 or 60 days, subject to the ceiling of 15 days in aggregate.

3. PRECEDENT APPLICATION (Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India (1978)) & RELIEF: Guided by Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India (1978), any executive or legislative overreach inconsistent with Article 22(1) is liable to be struck down or suitably moulded by appropriate directions. Applying the core concept of 'Default Bail', the impugned executive notification and show-cause order by the State Government Department must satisfy legality, rational nexus, and proportionality. As reinforced by Previous conviction is required for Article 20(2) (double jeopardy), not Article 20(3) (self-incrimination). Article 20(3) requires: (1) accused of an offense, (2) compulsion, and (3) testimonial evidence against oneself.

3. PRECEDENT APPLICATION (Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala (1973)) & RELIEF: Guided by Kesavananda Bharati v. legalTheme: Criminal Safeguards, Arrest & Custodial Rights (Articles 20 & 22) • Article 22(1) & Preventive Detention
factualMatrix: During proceedings before the Civil Judge (Senior Division) / District Court, Public Sector Undertaking / State Instrumentality defended an impugned statutory amendment and implementing rules enacted/issued in relation to Article 22(1) (Criminal Safeguards, Arrest & Custodial Rights (Articles 20 & 22)). The Respondent maintained that public interest and administrative necessity justified the measure, whereas the Petitioner demonstrated that Core constitutional framework under Criminal Safeguards, Arrest & Custodial Rights (Articles 20 & 22). The Bench was specifically called upon to reconcile the competing constitutional principles established in Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India (1978) with the Bare Act mandate of Article 22(1).
framingQuestions: 1. Whether the Original Civil Suit / Declaratory Relief before the Civil Judge (Senior Division) / District Court is maintainable in light of Article 22(1) and constitutional remedies?

2. How does the principle of Criminal Safeguards, Arrest & Custodial Rights (Articles 20 & 22) (Preventive Detention) apply to the impugned statutory amendment and implementing rules issued by the Public Sector Undertaking / State Instrumentality?
3. What is the controlling effect of Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India (1978) on the validity of the State/Respondent's action and what relief follows?
statutoryApplicability: Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India (1978)
modelAnswer:
1. MAINTAINABILITY & THRESHOLD (Article 22(1)): Under the constitutional scheme governing Criminal Safeguards, Arrest & Custodial Rights (Articles 20 & 22), a Original Civil Suit / Declaratory Relief before the Civil Judge (Senior Division) / District Court is maintainable where a prima facie breach of Article 22(1) or statutory/constitutional limits is demonstrated. The Court evaluates threshold jurisdiction without permitting procedural technicalities to defeat substantive constitutional justice.

2. DOCTRINAL & STATUTORY ANALYSIS (Criminal Safeguards, Arrest & Custodial Rights (Articles 20 & 22)): Core constitutional framework under Criminal Safeguards, Arrest & Custodial Rights (Articles 20 & 22). Applying the core concept of 'Preventive Detention', the impugned statutory amendment and implementing rules by the Public Sector Undertaking / State Instrumentality must satisfy legality, rational nexus, and proportionality. As reinforced by In Aslam Ahmed (1989) and Pramod Singla (2023), the Supreme Court reiterated that the right to make a representation under Article 22(5) includes the corresponding duty of the government to consider and dispose of it with reasonable dispatch. Unexplained delay vitiates the detention order and compels release.

3. PRECEDENT APPLICATION (Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India (1978)) & RELIEF: Guided by Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India (1978), any executive or legislative overreach inconsistent with Article 22(1) is liable to be struck down or suitably moulded by appropriate directions. Further, Under Harikisan v. State of Maharashtra (1962), communication of grounds under Article 22(5) means bringing the grounds to the actual understanding of the detainee. Providing documents in a language the detainee does not understand without an accurate translation vitiates the detention.

comprehensionMCQs.question: Scenario: A detainee under the Conservation of Foreign Exchange and Prevention of Smuggling Activities Act (COFEPOSA) submits a detailed representation to the Central Government on February 1. The representation reaches the ministry on February 5, where it lies on a clerk's table without being placed before the competent deciding authority until June 20. No explanation is offered for the delay. What is the constitutional effect under Article 22(5)?
options: The delay is a mere administrative irregularity and does not affect the detention order.
The unexplained delay of over 4 months constitutes an incurable violation of Article 22(5), rendering the continued detention illegal and entitling the detainee to immediate release on habeas corpus.
The detention period is automatically extended by 4 months to make up for lost time.
The detainee is entitled only to a refund of their legal fees from the department.
comprehensionMCQs.explanation: In Aslam Ahmed (1989) and Pramod Singla (2023), the Supreme Court reiterated that the right to make a representation under Article 22(5) includes the corresponding duty of the government to consider and dispose of it with reasonable dispatch. Unexplained delay vitiates the detention order and compels release.

comprehensionMCQs.question: Scenario: A truck driver who speaks and understands only Odia is placed under preventive detention. The grounds of detention and accompanying documents running into 80 pages are served on him exclusively in bureaucratic English. A constable merely reads the English document aloud. What did Harikisan v. State of Maharashtra hold regarding such communication?
options: Reading aloud in English is sufficient compliance with Article 22(5).

Supplying grounds in a language the detainee does not comprehend, without an effective translation, deprives the detainee of the constitutional right to make an effective representation, rendering the detention unconstitutional.
The driver has a duty to learn English while in detention.
The detention is valid because driving a truck requires basic knowledge of English road signs.
comprehensionMCQs.explanation: Under Harikisan v. State of Maharashtra (1962), communication of grounds under Article 22(5) means bringing the grounds to the actual understanding of the detainee. Providing documents in a language the detainee does not understand without an accurate translation vitiates the detention.
